pages.text: Ring Accelerators raise input particles to much higher energies than $(l:multiblocks/accelerators/linear_accelerator)Linear Accelerators$(/l), but cannot start an accelerator system. The system must begin with a Linear Accelerator using an $(l:multiblocks/accelerators/linear_accelerator#ion_source)Ion Source$(/l). $(bold)Ring Accelerators have a minimum input particle energy$(), usually 5 MeV by default.

pages.title: Construction
pages.text: Ring Accelerators are a square torus of Accelerator Casings or Glass that must be 5 blocks wide. Like all $(l:multiblocks/accelerators/general#construction)accelerators$(/l), they require Coolant Vents in input and output modes and an Energy Port. A continuous ring of Accelerator Beam Blocks runs down the center. Every beam port must connect to that central ring with a beam block.

Every corner and beam-port intersection requires a $(l:multiblocks/accelerators/general#dipole)Dipole Magnet$(/l), so a Ring Accelerator has at least four dipoles. The example above requires at least five.
Lastly, the inside corners of the accelerator must not be accelerator casing or accelerator glass. That area can instead be used to place certain coolers! Example below.

pages.title: Operation
pages.text: A Ring Accelerator operates like any other $(l:multiblocks/accelerators/general#operation)accelerator$(/l), requiring power and coolant. It requires an existing particle beam at or above the default 5 MeV minimum input energy. Ring Accelerators can have multiple beam ports, but only one input and one output can be active at a time. $(l:multiblocks/accelerators/beam_diverter#switching)Beam-port switching$(/l) uses redstone.

pages.title: Redstone Control
pages.text: As with the $(l:multiblocks/accelerators/linear_accelerator#redstone)Linear Accelerator$(/l), a redstone signal applied to the controller or an input $(l:multiblocks/accelerators/general#redstone)Redstone Port$(/l) turns it on, with output energy $(l)E=EₓSᵣ/15$().$(br2)Server integrations can set the percentage through the $(l:multiblocks/open_computers/introduction#accelerator_control)common state API$(/l).

pages.title: Particle Energy
pages.text: The resulting particle energy is more complicated to figure out than in a linear accelerator. The energy is limited by two factors, whichever factor is smaller will be the maximum particle output energy $(l)Eₓ=$(o)min$()$(l)(Eᵩ,Eᵣ)$(). These factors are from the dipole field strength and the synchrotron radiation losses.

pages.title: Max from Dipole Strength
pages.text: The maximum energy (in GeV) from dipole strength is $(l)Eᵩ=(qB₂R)²/(2m)$(), where $(l)q$() is particle charge, $(l)B₂$() is the sum of dipole strengths, $(l)R$() is the Ring Accelerator radius, and $(l)m$() is particle mass in MeV/c^2. For heavy particles such as protons, this is the main limit.

pages.title: Max from Radiation
pages.text: The maximum energy (in GeV) from the Radiation losses $(l)Eᵣ=m(3VR/|q|)⁰˙²⁵$() where $(l)V$() is the accelerator's voltage (in kV). For light particles like the electron this is the major concern.

Ring Accelerators can have one special Accelerator Synchrotron Port. It emits synchrotron radiation as high-energy photons. The same position rules as beam ports apply to Accelerator Synchrotron Ports.

Photon pu/t equals particle pu/t through the Ring Accelerator, and photon focus equals particle focus. Photon energy (in MeV) is $(l)Eᵧ=E³/(2πR(1000m)³)$(), where $(l)E$() is the output particle energy in MeV. $(br2)Because energy is proportional to $(l)1/m³$(), light particles such as electrons yield much higher energy.
